To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there were no differences in cognitive elaborations and information seeking between Twitterbots and human agents.
Twitterbots were compared for information seeking and affective learning to human agents.
there were no significant differences in perceptions of the communication quality of a Twitterbot and a human agent for information-seeking and learning outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of Twitterbots as agents for communication.
the use of Twitterbots as a communication medium.
the role of Twitterbots as social agents in social media environments, and how these agents may be used for information seeking and communication.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Twitterbots are not inferior to human agents in the areas of communication quality, cognitive elaboration, and information seeking.
Twitterbots are as effective as human agents in the areas of information seeking, cognitive elaboration, and affective learning.

Twitterbots and human agents are perceived to be equally effective in the areas of information seeking and learning, and that Twitterbots can potentially serve as effective agents for communication on Twitter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Twitterbots are effective communication tools in social media environments, and they may even be preferred by some users.
Twitterbots are not only capable of providing information, but can also be effective agents for information seeking in the areas of affective learning and cognitive elaboration.
Twitterbots are not significantly different from humans in the context of communication in social media.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Twitterbots may not be as bad as people think they are.
the CASA framework may not be a useful tool for predicting differences in perceptions of Twitterbot communication quality.
Twitterbots may be effective in communicating information and facilitating learning, and that the CASA framework may be a useful tool to understand the effects of social robots on learning.
